topic: Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Dialogue Between Religious & Non-Religious Beliefs
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are the two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: How do Theravada and Mahayana differ?

options.text: Theravada ('teaching of the elders') dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos — emphasises the Pali Canon and arhat ideal; Mahayana ('great vehicle') dominant in East Asia and Vietnam — emphasises bodhisattva path and Sanskrit/Chinese sutras; Tibetan Vajrayana is sometimes treated as a third stream

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal.

Tibetan Buddhism is often treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. The traditions share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the authoritative texts, and the role of devotion.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.
